description: Agreement clauses for a 13-15 year old. Not a scaled-up version of the clauses for seven year olds: at this age the phone is a social life, not a toy, and a rule imposed without a reason anyone understands gets worked around within a week. So every clause here carries its reason, and every clause on the teenager is matched by a heavier one on the parent — because a thirteen year old measures their parents precisely, and stops keeping their side the day they see the parents not keeping theirs.

pairs.child: No phones at the table — not even face-down next to my plate.
pairs.parent: No phones at the table, and I go first. If it rings, I let it ring.
pairs.note: The clause the whole agreement gets tested on. A teenager doesn't remember what you say; they remember what you do in front of them.

pairs.child: My phone sleeps outside my room, and the charger stays in the living room.
pairs.parent: My phone sleeps outside the bedroom too — no exception for me.
pairs.note: The most important health clause at this age. Sleep is the first thing a teenager loses, and it shows up in their schoolwork before it shows up in their mood.

pairs.child: If someone says something to me that bothers me or scares me, I tell them — even if I was in the wrong about something first.
pairs.parent: I hear you out without raising my voice, and I don't take your phone away the moment I hear it.
pairs.note: The most important clause in the whole product. A teenager who expects to lose their phone hides the problem until it grows — and taking the phone on the spot buys silence, not safety.

pairs.child: I don't meet anyone I met online without telling them, and never on my own.
pairs.parent: If they tell me they want to meet someone, I listen first and help them do it the right way — I don't refuse on the spot.
pairs.note: A flat refusal makes the meeting happen in secret. This clause is written to be workable, not to be comfortable.

pairs.child: Any new account I open, I tell them about.
pairs.parent: I don't get into their accounts behind their back. Being open is not being searched.
pairs.note: Here the pairing is the clause itself: the only teenager who tells you about a new account is the one who knows their parents aren't reading their messages in secret.

pairs.child: I don't post anyone's picture or anything they said without their okay — not even in a group chat.
pairs.parent: I don't put pictures of my kid anywhere without asking them.
pairs.note: The clause that surprises parents most. A thirteen year old knows exactly how many pictures of them are up without their okay, and will bring it up in the first argument.

pairs.child: During study time my phone is in another room, not face-down on the desk.
pairs.parent: I don't interrupt them while they're studying to show them something on my phone.
pairs.note: Parents interrupt more than they admit, and having it in the clause is what makes the ask fair.

pairs.child: I don't buy anything online without asking — not even when it's free and asks for my information.
pairs.parent: If they slip up and spend money, we talk about the fix, not about punishment.
pairs.note: "Free and asks for my information" is the more important half of the clause: at this age the scams come from free games, not from stores.

pairs.child: We go over this agreement every month, and I have the right to ask for a clause to change.
pairs.parent: We actually go over it every month, and if they ask for a change I hear them out and talk it through — I don't put it off.
pairs.note: An agreement that never gets reviewed turns into an old list of orders. And the right to ask is what makes a teenager a party to it rather than someone it was signed over.
